SCT सोबत २० -२५ % केमिकल खते व आपत्कालीन परिस्थितीत १०% औषधांचा वापर करावा लागत होता‼️

   मित्रहो ,
 साधे सरळ सुत्र आहे, आपण हायब्रिड व्हरायट्यांची शेती करतो मग ती फळबाग असो की भाजीपाला वा धान्य शेती‼️

मित्रहो ,
   गेल्या ६-७ वर्षांत सॉइल चार्जर टेक्नोलॉजी च्या मदतीने आपन शेतीला रासायनिक कडून विषमुक्ती कडे नेण्यास ९५% यशस्वी झालेलो आहोत‼️

  जरी  SCT वैदीक हे आपल्याला नविन वाटत असेल तरी ते भारतीयांसाठी नवीन नाही , आपले पुर्वजांनी रितीरिवाज , सणउत्सव यांमध्ये वैदीक विधींचा दैनंदीन जिवनात व शेतीत पुर्वीपासून अवलंब केलेला आहे ‼️

     अगदी राज्य व प्रदेशानुसार जेवनातील विशेष खाद्यपदार्थांची निवड असो ‼️

  मित्रहो,

     हा अत्यंत महत्त्वाचा नियम आहे ‼️

    SCT वैदीक मधील उत्पादने पिकातील व मातीतील उर्जा न वापरता मोठ्या प्रमाणात उर्जेचे भांडार उपलब्ध करतात, हे या तंत्रज्ञानाचे खास वैशिष्टय आहे‼️

     मुळातच सिंथेटीक ( कृत्रीम ) फर्टिलायझर्स (खते ) मातीतील जीवांचे  किंवा पिकांचे अन्नच नाही ते हायब्रिड व्हरायट्यांना सेन्स ( ज्ञान ) नसल्यामुळे भुकेपोटी शोषले जातात‼️
   जर हे केमिकल खते सहजासहजी शोषले गेले नाही तर शेतकरी पिजीआर वापरून पिकाला पुर्णपणे बेहोश करतात आणि  पिकाकडून जबरदस्ती अपटेक करून घेतात‼️

     खरंतर याच कारणामुळे केमिकल शेतीचे वर्तमान व भविष्य धोक्यात आलेले आहे‼️
   एकीकडे निसर्गाचा मार , दुसरीकडे ग्राहकांचा तिरस्कार अशा दुहेरी कात्रीत केमिकल शेती सापडली आहे‼️

   कारण सेंद्रीय अवशेष किंवा जिवाणू हायब्रीड व्हरायट्यांची राक्षसी भूक भागविन्यास असमर्थ आहेत‼️

      याला काही प्रमाणात अपवाद आहे , द्राक्ष, आंबा , डाळींब , संत्री  व इतर फळबाग शेती , कारण जर तुम्ही बहुवर्षीय पिकांवर वाटर  सोल्यूबल  , पिजीआर ( जीए , सायटोकायनीन्स वगैरे ) व विषारी बुरशीनाशके यांचा अतिरेकी वापर केला तर त्या मातीवर नाही तर झाडांच्या डीएन ए वर दूरगामी परिणाम होतात ‼️
    SCTवैदीक वापरन्यापुर्वी शेतकरी हा विचार करत नाहीत की आपण मातीचे किती शोषण केले , पीएच ईसी किती वाढला , सेंद्रिय कर्ब किती घसरला , आपण मातीचे अगदी वाळवंट करत आनले , वरतून अशा निकस व दुषीत मातीत बाग घेऊन त्यावर पीजीआर व वाटरसोल्यूबल ची केमिकल खते वापरून त्या बागेतील झाडांचा डीएनए कमजोर केलेला आहे‼️
     SCTवैदीक तुम्ही यापुर्वी केलेले मातीचे नुकसान आणि झाडांचे कुपोषण याची जबाबदारी शेतकरी उचलत नाही, त्यांना रिझल्ट मात्र आज आत्ता ताबडतोब पाहीजे असतो , त्यांनी यापुर्वी केलेले खड्डे भरून काढल्या शिवाय वैदीकचे परिणाम प्रभावी पणे दिसत नाही‼️

    शेतकर्यांना आमचे ओफीसर सांगतात की  SCTवैदीक तंत्रज्ञान अवगत होईपर्यंत तुम्ही थोड्या क्षेत्रावर वापर करा , परंतू युट्यूब वरचे रिझल्ट पाहून अती उत्साही शेतकर्यांना १००% बागेवर वापरुन फायदा करून घ्यायचा असतो ,

After reading the title You might be confused about what that even means. India’s been dependent on farming for thousands of years, it isn’t going to die anytime soon. Yeah, you are right about most of the part but more than just agriculture we have always been dependent on farmers till today. 60% of the Indian population is still dependent on agriculture contributing to 18% of Countries GDP.

But still, even being an agriculture-dependent country why are so many farmers still not satisfied and what are the problems farmers face nowadays?

I the past days we have farmers take their stand and demand for help. From the fertile lands of Punjab arises a movement that echoes across the nation – the farmers' protest. In Punjab, where agriculture is not just a livelihood but a way of life, farmers have taken a stand for their rights and the future of farming. Let's lend our support to their cause, recognizing their resilience and unwavering spirit in the face of challenges.

But Why? What are the things going wrong about the Agricultural industry?

Here are some of the Major Problems faced by Farmers:

Lack Of Storage Facilities

Even after being the largest Milk and pulse Producer and Second largest Vegetable, Rice and Fruit producer in the world we still have such a fragile storage facility. Poor Logistics and Inferior Warehousing facilities lead to wastage and huge financial losses for farmers.

The lack of Storage has forced farmers to stand for their rights and demand the help they deserve

One potential arrangement is for the government to put resources into building more storage foundations, like cold storage units and stockrooms. Moreover, the public authority could boost privately owned businesses to put resources into storerooms by giving tax reductions or different advantages. Another methodology is to further develop transportation, like streets and rail routes, to empower quicker and more effective vehicles of produce to business sectors. At last, the public authority could likewise advance the reception of present-day agrarian practices, like yield broadening and further developed collecting methods, to diminish the amount of produce that should be put into storage.

Lack Of Mechanization

The lack of Mechanization in the agricultural sector has raised a lot of concerns in the modern world. Despite strides made in various industries, traditional farming methods still prevail in many regions. Farmers continue to rely on manual labour, often with basic tools and outdated techniques, leading to inefficiencies and limited productivity.

This reliance on manual labour not only perpetuates poverty among small-scale farmers but also exacerbates social and economic disparities. The absence of mechanization prevents farmers from maximizing their yields and adapting to changing environmental conditions. Furthermore, it contributes to the migration of rural populations to urban centres in search of better opportunities, straining already overburdened cities.

Environmental sustainability is another concern, as outdated farming practices contribute to soil degradation, water scarcity, and loss of biodiversity. Without access to modern machinery and technology, farmers struggle to implement precision agriculture techniques that could minimize environmental impact and optimize resource use.

Investment in mechanization and modern farming techniques is crucial for India's agricultural sector to meet the challenges of the 21st century. By providing farmers with access to affordable machinery, training, and support, India can enhance agricultural productivity, improve livelihoods, and ensure food security for its growing population. Additionally, embracing sustainable farming practices can mitigate environmental degradation and build resilience against the impacts of climate change.

Bad Credit Availability

Credit availability for farmers in India faces several challenges, contributing to the overall inadequacy and ineffectiveness of agricultural credit systems. Here are some key reasons why credit availability for farmers is often insufficient or problematic in India:

1. Many small-scale and marginalized farmers in India have limited access to formal banking institutions due to factors such as geographic remoteness, lack of collateral, and low financial literacy. As a result, they often rely on informal sources of credit, such as local moneylenders, who charge exorbitant interest rates, trapping farmers in cycles of debt.

2. Formal financial institutions often impose stringent eligibility criteria for agricultural loans, such as land ownership and credit history, which many smallholder farmers cannot meet. This excludes a significant portion of the farming population from accessing institutional credit, forcing them to seek alternative, often exploitative, sources of financing.

3. While the Indian government has implemented various agricultural credit schemes to support farmers, the allocation of credit often falls short of the actual demand. Limited budgetary allocations, bureaucratic inefficiencies, and corruption can hinder the effective distribution of credit, leaving many farmers undeserved.

4. Agricultural loans in India are often considered risky due to factors such as unpredictable weather patterns, crop failures, and market fluctuations. This perceived risk leads banks to prioritize other sectors over agriculture, resulting in lower credit availability for farmers. Additionally, high levels of loan defaults and NPAs in the agricultural sector further deter financial institutions from extending credit to farmers.

5. Despite efforts to promote financial inclusion in rural areas through initiatives like Jan Dhan Yojana and PMJDY, many farmers still lack access to formal banking services. Limited infrastructure, inadequate banking facilities, and low awareness about available financial products contribute to the persistence of financial exclusion among rural communities.

Depletion In Soil Fertility

The widespread use of chemical fertilizers in modern agriculture has led to a concerning depletion of soil fertility, posing a significant threat to global food security and environmental sustainability. These synthetic inputs, initially lauded for their role in boosting crop yields, have become a double-edged sword, exacting a toll on the very soil they were intended to nourish.

Nitrogen-based fertilizers do provide a vital nutrient for the plant but use of it leads to soil with unbalanced pH and contamination of water bodies and aquatic life. The use of these fertilizers has always resulted in the degradation of soil still farmers continue to use it cause of faster results without thinking of consequences.

Phosphorus composts, fundamental for plant root improvement and energy movement, present a comparable problem. Their abuse prompts soil immersion, decreasing its ability to ingest and hold supplements. The abundance of phosphorus drains into streams, causing eutrophication and environmental debasement, intensifying the issue.

Potassium composts, however frequently neglected, add to soil debasement when applied unnecessarily. Soil pH, nutrient availability, and structure are all altered by high potassium levels, making it more susceptible to erosion and compaction.

To address this crisis, a shift towards sustainable agricultural practices is imperative. Embracing organic farming methods, cover cropping, crop rotation, and integrated nutrient management can help replenish soil nutrients, restore soil health, and ensure long-term agricultural sustainability. By breaking free from the dependency on chemical fertilizers, farmers can cultivate a future where soil fertility thrives, sustaining bountiful harvests for generations to come.

Price Volatility

The volatility in the Indian agriculture market is a multifaceted issue rooted in various factors, ranging from structural inefficiencies to external market forces. One primary reason for this volatility is the lack of efficient market infrastructure and distribution networks. India's agricultural supply chain is characterized by fragmentation, with numerous intermediaries between farmers and consumers, leading to price distortions and inefficiencies.

Furthermore, India's dependence on monsoon rains for agricultural production makes the sector highly susceptible to weather-related risks. Erratic rainfall patterns, droughts, and floods can lead to significant fluctuations in crop yields, impacting market supply and prices.

Government policies and regulations also play a crucial role in shaping market dynamics. Price support mechanisms, such as minimum support prices (MSPs), aim to provide farmers with assured incomes; however, they can distort market prices and create surpluses, leading to storage issues and downward pressure on prices during bumper harvests.

Additionally, India's agriculture sector is heavily influenced by global market trends, including fluctuations in commodity prices and currency exchange rates. Imports and exports of agricultural commodities are subject to international market dynamics, exposing Indian farmers to price volatility beyond their control.

Moreover, information asymmetry and lack of access to market data exacerbate price volatility, making it difficult for farmers to make informed decisions about when and where to sell their produce.

Addressing these challenges requires a holistic approach encompassing policy reforms, investment in infrastructure, technology adoption, and risk management strategies. Strengthening market linkages, promoting value addition, and enhancing farmer access to information and credit can help mitigate price volatility and improve income stability for Indian farmers in the long run.

These were some of the reasons why Indian farmers are still not satisfied with being only dependent on agriculture. If we want to change the lives of the majority of Indian farmers government should work on these types of topics and work in favour of farmers. That is the only way to help farmers today.
